title: Financial Literacy
description: Manage everyday money: budgeting, debt, an emergency fund, and investing for a calmer life.

stations.title: Building a Budget
stations.summary: A budget is not a prison, it is a map. You control money; money does not control you.
points: The 50/30/20 guide: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt repayment.
Track every expense for 30 days — the biggest leak is usually a surprise.
Pay yourself first: move savings at the start of the month, not from whatever is left.
Overly strict budgets rarely survive; leave room for small things that keep you happy.

questions.prompt: Income is 4,000,000 a month. Using the 50/30/20 guide, how much should go to essential needs?
questions.explain: 50% of 4,000,000 is 2,000,000 for essentials such as food, rent, electricity, and transport.

questions.prompt: Why is it better to save at the beginning of the month?
options: Because banks calculate interest at the start of the month
So savings are not eaten up by other spending first
Because banks are closed at month end
So the money can be withdrawn immediately
questions.explain: Pay yourself first: if you wait for the leftover, there is often nothing left.

questions.prompt: The most sensible first step before building a budget is...
options: Immediately cutting all entertainment spending
Recording your actual spending for a month
Borrowing money to cover the shortfall
Opening accounts at many banks
questions.explain: Without real spending data a budget is just a guess. Measure first, then cut the biggest leaks.

cards.back: Save at the start of the month, not from what is left over

stations.title: Debt & Interest
stations.summary: Debt can help or trap you — the difference lies in purpose, interest, and your ability to repay.
points: Tell productive debt apart (business capital, education) from consumer debt (gadgets, holidays).
Compound interest cuts both ways: it rewards savers and punishes borrowers.
A safe instalment load is generally no more than 30% of monthly income.
Read the total amount you will pay, not just the monthly instalment.

questions.prompt: A 10,000,000 loan at 2% interest per month, repaid over 12 months. Roughly how much interest in a year?
questions.explain: 2% × 10,000,000 = 200,000 per month. Over 12 months ≈ 2,400,000 (simple calculation, ignoring the shrinking principal).

questions.prompt: Which one is best described as productive debt?
options: Credit card spending on clothes
A loan to capitalise a small food stall
Instalments for the newest phone
Borrowing to eat out often
questions.explain: Productive debt creates value or income, so the instalments can be covered by what it generates.

questions.prompt: The commonly used safe limit for total instalments is...
options: 10% of income
30% of income
60% of income
Anything, as long as you pay the minimum
questions.explain: Above roughly 30% of income, the room for essentials and emergencies becomes too tight.

cards.back: Creates value or income: business capital, education, work tools
Around 30% of monthly income at most

stations.title: Emergency Fund
stations.summary: An emergency fund is your safety brake: it keeps you calm when the unexpected happens.
points: Common target: 3–6 times your monthly expenses (closer to 6–12 if income is irregular).
Keep it somewhere safe and easy to cash out, not in something whose value swings.
It is not for huge discounts — that belongs to your wants budget.
Top it up again after use, however small the amount.

questions.prompt: Monthly expenses are 3,000,000. What is the minimum emergency fund target (3 months)?
questions.explain: 3 × 3,000,000 = 9,000,000 as the first layer of protection.

questions.prompt: The best place to keep an emergency fund is...
options: Wherever returns are highest, even if it is hard to withdraw
Safe, liquid, and available at any time
Locked in for at least five years
Something whose value rises and falls with the market
questions.explain: The point of an emergency fund is to be usable immediately, not to grow the fastest.

questions.prompt: Which situation is the emergency fund really for?
options: A 70% discount at the electronics store
Sudden medical costs
An end-of-year holiday
Buying a new vehicle
questions.explain: It covers urgent, unexpected events, especially health costs and loss of income.

stations.title: Investing & Inflation
stations.summary: Saving keeps your money; investing protects its buying power. You need both — in the right order.
points: Inflation pushes prices up: money that only sits slowly loses purchasing power.
Higher potential returns always come with higher risk — no exceptions.
Understand an instrument before buying it; if you do not, that is speculation.
Be wary of promises of large, fixed, fast profits.

options: Prices rise by about 5% a year on average
Your money grows by 5% a year
Prices fall by 5% a year
Bank interest is definitely 5% a year
questions.explain: Inflation is a general rise in prices. If savings earn 2% while inflation is 5%, your purchasing power falls.

questions.prompt: The clearest red flag in an investment offer is...
options: It comes with written documents
It promises large, guaranteed, fast returns
It explains its risks
It asks you to study the product first
questions.explain: Legitimate investments never guarantee returns. 'Fixed, fast, big' is the classic fraud pattern.

questions.prompt: The wisest order before you start investing is...
options: Invest first, build the emergency fund later
Emergency fund ready, high-interest consumer debt cleared, then invest
Go straight into high-risk instruments
Just follow a friend's tip without reading anything
questions.explain: Build the foundation first: emergency fund and expensive debt, then invest based on goals and risk profile.

cards.back: A general rise in prices; cash loses buying power over time
